findings.title: Valid backup code plus any dummy totpCode logs in without a password
findings.body:
The password check at line 121 runs only when `credentials.totpCode` is empty (`if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)`). The new branch at line 131 then takes priority over TOTP whenever `credentials.backupCode` is set, and the TOTP code is never checked.

So an attacker can POST to the credentials callback with the victim's email, `totpCode=000000` and one valid backup code. The password check is skipped, the junk TOTP is never validated, and the backup code alone grants a session. Backup codes are offered as a plaintext download (`cal-backup-codes.txt`) and via the clipboard, so leaking one is realistic. This reduces 2FA to a single factor that is easier to steal than the password.

Fix: always verify the password for CAL users when a backup code is used. Better still, reject requests that carry both `totpCode` and `backupCode`, and stop tying password verification to the absence of `totpCode`.

findings.title: Backup code consumption is non-atomic read-check-write (single-use not guaranteed)
findings.body:
The handler reads `user.backupCodes`, decrypts it, finds the index, nulls that entry, then writes the whole re-encrypted blob back with a plain `update`. Nothing checks that the stored value is still the one that was read.

Two concurrent login requests with the same backup code can both pass `indexOf` before either write lands, so a code meant to be used "exactly once" can open several sessions.

A concurrent use of a different code can also be lost (last write wins), which leaves an already-used code valid.

Fix: do a conditional update, e.g. `updateMany` with `where: { id, backupCodes: <original ciphertext> }`, and fail if `count === 0`. Alternatively, store codes in a separate table and delete the row atomically.

findings.title: Dismissing the backup-codes step via Escape/overlay never calls onEnable, leaving stale UI state
findings.body:
After a successful enable, the modal now moves to `DisplayBackupCodes` instead of calling `onEnable()`. Only the custom "Close" button calls `onEnable()`.

The Dialog can also be closed through `onOpenChange` (Escape key, overlay click, the X). That path just toggles `open` in the parent, so `onEnable` never runs. 2FA is already enabled on the server, yet the settings switch keeps showing it as disabled: the `me` query is not invalidated and the success toast never fires.

The component's `step` also stays at `DisplayBackupCodes`. Reopening the modal shows the old codes with no Cancel button. If the user instead retries enabling, `setup` returns `TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled`, which the modal shows as "something went wrong".

Fix: handle `onOpenChange` while on the backup-codes step (call `onEnable` and `resetState`), or block dismissal on that step.

findings.title: Existing 2FA users get a 'Lost access' option with no codes and are pointed to a settings feature that doesn't exist
findings.body:
Backup codes are only generated in `setup.ts` during a new 2FA setup. Every user who already has 2FA enabled has `backupCodes = NULL`.

The login page and the disable modal still show them the "Lost access" button. Using it returns `MissingBackupCodes`, whose message reads "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." This PR adds no way to generate or regenerate backup codes in settings. The only route is to disable and re-enable 2FA, which the locked-out user cannot do.

Once all 10 codes are used, the stored array holds only nulls, so the user gets `IncorrectBackupCode` rather than any hint that the codes are exhausted.

Fix: either add a regenerate-codes feature, or reword the message and hide "Lost access" when no codes exist.

findings.title: No test covers logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code, or single-use consumption
Backup codes stored reversibly encrypted instead of hashed
findings.body:
Backup codes are stored as `symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(codes), CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)`. Unlike the TOTP secret, the server never needs the plaintext codes back; it only has to check that a submitted code matches.

With reversible encryption, anyone who obtains a DB dump plus the encryption key (one env var, shared with other secrets) gets every user's usable bypass codes.

Store a salted hash per code (e.g. bcrypt/argon2 or HMAC) and compare hashes on use.

findings.title: Uppercase placeholder suggests uppercase codes, but matching is case-sensitive against lowercase hex
findings.body:
Codes are generated with `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")`, so they are lowercase. Both `next-auth-options.ts` and `disable.ts` compare with `indexOf(code.replaceAll("-", ""))`, which is an exact, case-sensitive match with no trimming.

The input placeholder is `XXXXX-XXXXX`. A user who types a code from paper in uppercase, or pastes one with surrounding whitespace, is rejected as "Backup code is incorrect."

Normalize input with `.trim().toLowerCase()` before comparing.

findings.title: Copy shows a success toast without awaiting the clipboard, and crashes where the Clipboard API is unavailable
findings.body:
The `navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` promise is not awaited, so "Backup codes copied!" appears even when the write is rejected (permission denied).

On self-hosted instances served over plain HTTP on a non-localhost host, `navigator.clipboard` is `undefined`. The click handler then throws a TypeError and nothing is copied.

Await the promise, show an error toast on failure, and guard for a missing `navigator.clipboard`.

findings.title: Password visibility toggle removed from keyboard tab order app-wide
findings.body:
Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide password button in the shared `PasswordField` makes it unreachable by keyboard. This affects every password field in the app, not just the 2FA modals.

Keyboard-only and assistive-technology users can no longer reveal their password. This is an accessibility regression unrelated to backup codes.
